name: Jerusalem (from Haifa , Israel)

sights.name: Church of Our Lady of the Covenant
sights.content: Located at the north-west part of the village of Abu Ghosh. The church is located at the summit of Tel Kiryat Ye'arim. The site is identified with the biblical Kiryat Ye'arim, where the [[:w:Ark of Covenant

sights.name: The Benedictine monastery in Abu Ghosh
sights.content: It is best known for the Crusader church that contains remains of a 12th-century frescoes. The church was built over a spring. Abu Ghosh's main mosque is adjacent to the monastery.

foodDrink.name: Tel Aviv University
foodDrink.content: The largest proper university in Israel (the Open University, though larger, is for distance learning and does not grant doctorates), situated in Ramat Aviv.

foodDrink.name: Tel Aviv-Jaffa Academic College
foodDrink.content: A smaller college in Tel Aviv

foodDrink.name: Afeka
foodDrink.content: Tel Aviv Academic College of Engineering

foodDrink.name: Ulpan Bayit
foodDrink.content:
Private Hebrew language school (ulpan) in the Florentin neighbourhood, founded in 2013. Intensive, morning and evening Hebrew courses at all levels for
newcomers and visitors, plus online classes.

foodDrink.name: HaAmbatia
foodDrink.content: Language and culture school teaching spoken Arabic, French, German, Italian and Spanish in small groups. Classes are aimed at Hebrew speakers.

foodDrink.name: United States
foodDrink.content: This is considered to be a branch office, as the U.S. maintains its official embassy to Israel in Jerusalem.

dayTrips: Dead Sea (Israel and the West Bank)
missing: a mapped cruise terminal or pier

cityEats.name: Panoramic Golden City Restaurant Cafe Roof

guideSights.name: The Western Wall
guideSights.note: Part of the western retaining wall of the Temple Mount, it was built by Herod the Great during his expansion of the Temple in 20 BCE. The wall became the Jews' chief place of pilgrimage during the Ottoman Period. In this period it become kn

guideSights.name: Western Wall Tunnel Tour
guideSights.note: This is a tour of the underground parts of the Western Wall, including the evolution of the Temple Mount from the First Temple period to today. A wonderful tour for those interested in the archeology and history of the Temple Mount. You wil

guideSights.name: Saint Mary's Hospice
guideSights.note: The ruins of a 12th-century German Crusader Hospice within view of the Temple Mount. Worth a short visit. A Jewish art gallery/shop is to the left of the door to the hospice's church (it's pretty obvious which of the buildings is the church

guideSights.name: The Cardo
guideSights.note: Once running nearly the entire length of the Old City from north to south, the Cardo is an excavated and partially reconstructed section of the Jerusalem's main thoroughfare in the Byzantine era. Visitors can get a good idea of how the whol

guideSights.name: Hurva Square
guideSights.note: In a maze of narrow and winding streets, Hurva Square is the heart and social center of the Jewish Quarter. Its open areas offer cafes, souvenir shops, and snack bars with outdoor seating. On the west side of the square is the site of the H

guideSights.name: The Broad Wall
guideSights.note: Following the 1967 Israeli victory, a vast reconstruction program in the Jewish Quarter resulted in many important archaeological finds. One of the most significant was the unearthing of the foundations of a massive wall. These fortificatio

guideSights.name: Burnt House
guideSights.note: This house was inhabited by a wealthy priestly family at the end of the Second Temple period, and burned down by the Romans in 70 CE.

guideSights.name: Davidson Center
guideSights.note: This area on the southern side of the Temple Mount had been rebuilt many times over the centuries. Remains from the Herodian (34–4 BCE), Byzantine (395–661 CE) and Omayyad (661–750 CE) periods can be found on the grounds.

guideSights.name: Karaite Synagogue
guideSights.note: The Karaite Jews, numbering 30-50,000 worldwide, are a unique sect of Judaism that has been at odds with mainstream rabbinic Judaism for centuries. The Karaites reject the Talmud (Oral Law) and only rely on the Torah, Prophets, and Writings

guideSights.name: Wohl Archaeological Museum
guideSights.note: Lying 3 to 7 m (10 to 22 ft) below street level, this museum offers a vivid excavation of daily life during the Herodian era 2,000 years ago, before the Romans rampaged and burned the wealthy Upper City in AD 70. Photography inside the muse

guideSights.name: Temple Institute
guideSights.note: A fairly interesting place which has reconstructed most of the more obvious ritual tools to be used in the Temple services in the hopes of one day restoring the Temple itself. The front of the store is a bookstore/souvenir shop, while the b

guideSights.name: Old Yishuv Court Museum
guideSights.note: The history of the Jewish community in the Jewish Quarter of Jerusalem from the beginning of the 15th century until the fall of the Quarter in the War of Independence.

guideSights.name: Tower of David/Citadel
guideSights.note: Now occupied by the ''Tower of David Museum of the History of Jerusalem'', the Citadel is an imposing fortress inside the city wall beside the Jaffa Gate. Utilized and expanded throughout the centuries as a means of protection, excavations

guideSights.name: St. James Cathedral
guideSights.note: This Armenian cathedral is one of the most beautiful of all the sacred buildings in Jerusalem. It was constructed in the 11th and 12th centuries over the traditional tomb of St James the Apostle. Attending an Armenian Orthodox vespers servi

guideSights.name: Saint Mark's Syriac Church and Monastery
guideSights.note: The monastery is open all day, simply ring at the gate. According to tradition, this church was built on the site of the house of Mary, mother of St Mark. Every weekday the three resident monks hold the 25-minute vespers service at 16:00 fo

guideSights.name: Armenian Museum
guideSights.note: Located slightly down the street from Saint James Cathedral, it is housed in what was once either the monastery or the guest house for the Armenian Monastery of Saint James. The museum holds an impressive and very well documented collection
guideSights.en: Mardigian Museum of Armenian Art and Culture

guideSights.name: Church of the Holy Sepulchre
guideSights.note: The Holy Sepulchre is a large building spanning several areas in which Christ is believed by Christians to have been crucified and died, was buried, and then rose from the dead on the third day. Eastern Orthodox Christians, Roman Catholi

guideSights.name: Lutheran Church of the Redeemer
guideSights.note: This church was built by Kaiser Wilhelm II and completed in 1898. The church is most admired by tourists for its bell tower. At the top of its 177 steps, visitors are rewarded with some great views over the Old City. Below the church there

guideSights.name: Christian Quarter Road
guideSights.note: Along with David Street, is the quarter's main shopping thoroughfare. As with most shopping areas in the Christian Quarter, it specializes in religious items as well as handicrafts.

guideSights.name: Muristan
guideSights.note: Just south of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, this area was once a hospice for pilgrims from Latin-speaking countries. Today it serves as a quiet area of outdoor cafes and small shops centered around an atmospheric central fountain.

guideSights.name: Church of St John the Baptist
guideSights.note: Adorned by a silvery dome, this church is visible from the Muristan even though the entrance is fairly difficult to locate. Founded in the 5th century, the church is significant as one of the most ancient churches in Jerusalem. The church w
guideSights.en: Church of Saint John the Baptist, Jerusalem

guideSights.name: A Walk on the Roofs
guideSights.note: It is possible to walk above the central souk along the rooftops of the city. Visitors can climb up to the rooftops via a small staircase at the corner of St Mark's Road and Khabad Street. A second set of stairs leads up from Muristan Road

guideSights.name: St. Anne's Church
guideSights.note: This Crusader-era church was built between 1131 and 1138 to replace a Byzantine church. It is traditionally believed to be the spot where Anne and Joachim, the parents of the Virgin Mary, lived. the church fell into ruins until it was donat

guideSights.name: Monastery of the Flagellation
guideSights.note: Owned by the Franciscans, this site is traditionally held to be where Christ was flogged by Roman soldiers prior to his crucifixion. Opposite the courtyard is the '''Chapel of the Condemnation''', built on the site popularly identified with

guideSights.name: Ecce Homo Arch
guideSights.note: This arch, which spans the Via Dolorosa, was built by the Romans in AD 70 to support a ramp for the attack on the Antonia Fortress. The arch was reconstructed as a monument to victory when the Romans rebuilt Jerusalem in AD 135. Incorporate

guideSights.name: Zedekiah's Cave
guideSights.note: A large quarry underneath the Old City. Used for several thousand years; the stones of the Western Wall were likely carved from here. Entrance is from just outside the Old City walls, a bit east of Damascus Gate.

guideSights.name: Dome of the Rock
guideSights.note: (Arabic: Qubbat Al-Sakhra, Hebrew: Kippat HaSela), located in the middle of the sanctuary opposite of the Al-Aqsa Mosque, is probably the most dazzling and well-known landmark of Jerusalem, with its golden dome and octagonal blue walls ador

guideSights.name: al-Aqsa Mosque
guideSights.note: The point from where Mohammad is believed to have ascended to heaven. This association has made the building the third-holiest site in Islam after Mecca and Medina. Construction of the mosque began less than 20 years after the completion of

guideSights.name: Museum of Islamic Art
guideSights.note: Housed in the Crusader-era refectory of the Knights Templar, this filled museum contains wonderful Islamic architectural remnants. An admission is required, but it is recommended that guests interested in Islamic art visit the LA Mayer Muse

guideSights.name: Golden Gate Interior
guideSights.note: on the east wall of the Temple Mount/Haram esh-Sharif. According to Jewish tradition the Messiah will arrive in the Temple via this gate, and according to Christian tradition Jesus entered through this gate on Palm Sunday. Closed by the Mus

guideSights.name: Church of the Dormition
guideSights.note: Adorned by a conical dome and a tall bell tower, this Mount Zion church is the traditional site of the Virgin Mary's death. Several churches have been built on the site. The present-day structure was built in the early 20th century for the

guideSights.name: King David's Tomb
guideSights.note: Adjoining the Church of the Dormition and located on the lower floor of the Crusader building is a small chamber venerated as King David's Tomb. The chamber—divided for separate viewing by men and women—contains a sarcophagus co

guideSights.name: Last Supper Room
guideSights.note: A room in the David's Tomb Compound, traditionally held to be the site of the Last Supper.

guideSights.name: Chamber of the Holocaust
guideSights.note: Located directly opposite the Tomb of David on Mount Zion, this small museum is maintained by the Diaspora Yeshiva. The collection includes Holocaust artifacts, artwork inspired by the Holocaust, an exhibit of anti-Semitic publications thro

guideSights.name: Schindler's Tomb
guideSights.note: Down the hill from the Zion Gate is a small Christian cemetery. It is here that the grave of Oskar Schindler is located. Schindler, a German industrialist, saved 1,200 Jews from the Holocaust by hiring them as laborers in his factory. The s

guideSights.name: St Peter in Gallicantu
guideSights.note: Located to the east of Mount Zion and overlooking the Kidron Valley, this church commemorates the traditional site of St Peter's denial of Christ. In the crypt below the church are ancient caves, purported to be the place where Christ spent
guideSights.en: Church of St. Peter in Gallicantu

guideSights.name: City of David and Jerusalem water system
guideSights.note: To get here, exit the Old City through Dung Gate (by the Kotel), turn left, and then take the first street on your right. The site comprises two archeological findings.

guideSights.name: Tomb of Absalom
guideSights.note: An impressive burial monument, approximately 20 meters tall, that is mistakenly attributed to King David's rebellious son Absalom. It is in the valley between the Old City and the Mount of Olives. Just to the south is the so-called '''Tomb

guideSights.name: Chapel of the Ascension
guideSights.note: Sacred to Christians and Muslims, this medieval chapel—now part of a mosque—is on the supposed site of Christ's ascension. The chapel was built around 380 AD around a venerated imprint, now set in stone, of Christ's right foot. The chapel b

guideSights.name: Church of the Pater Noster
guideSights.note: Built over Constantine-era ruins, this church sits atop a grotto where Christ is believed to have taught the Paternoster (meaning "Our Father"), or Lord's Prayer. The church is famous for its tiled panels inscribed with the Lord's Prayer in

guideSights.name: Seven Arches Hotel Viewpoint
guideSights.note: Near the Seven Arches hotel, definitely the best view of the Old City of Jerusalem. Come here to take panoramic pictures and be stunned by the beauty of the city.

guideSights.name: Tombs of the Prophets
guideSights.note: At the top of the Jewish Cemetery, which spans the southwestern slope of the Mount of Olives, lies a large catacomb complex containing oven-shaped graves (kokhim). The Palestinian family which discovered the catacomb claims that the tombs b
guideSights.en: Tomb of the Prophets Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi

guideSights.name: Mount of Olives Jewish Cemetery
guideSights.note: The most ancient and most important cemetery in Jerusalem. Burial on the Mount of Olives started some 3,000 years ago in the First Temple Period, and continues to this day. Famous figures in Jewish history are buried here, including Nachman

guideSights.name: Dominus Flevit Chapel
guideSights.note: Its name meaning "The Lord Wept", this chapel was identified by medieval pilgrims as the place where Jesus wept over the fate of Jerusalem. The chapel's west window frames a breathtaking view of the Old City. A small collection of stone art

guideSights.name: Church of St. Mary Magdalene
guideSights.note: This Russian Orthodox Church, with its gilded onion domes, was built by Tsar Alexander III in 1885 in memory of his mother, Maria Alexandrovna, whose patron saint was Mary Magdalene. Tsar Alexander III's sister-in-law, Grand Duchess Elizabe

guideSights.name: Church of All Nations and Garden of Gethsemane
guideSights.note: Also known as the Church of Agony because it is built over the rock where Jesus agonized about his death, this 4th-century church has been rebuilt many times, the most recent structure being the result of financial contributions from 12 nat

guideSights.name: Tomb of the Virgin / Cave of Gethsemane
guideSights.note: Directly across from the Church of All Nations, the Tomb of the Virgin is believed to be where the Disciples entombed Mary, the mother of Jesus. Forty-seven steps lead past side niches and down to crypt, which contains the burial place of Q

guideSights.name: Rockefeller Archaeological Museum
guideSights.note: The Rockefeller Museum was made possible by a substantial contribution by American oil tycoon John D. Rockefeller. The museum houses an impressive collection of antiquities, including a number of the Dead Sea Scrolls.

guideSights.name: Garden Tomb
guideSights.note: Disputed to be an alternative to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre as the location of the death, burial and resurrection of Christ, the Garden Tomb is located a block north of the Damascus Gate. British general, Charles Gordon, popularized t

guideSights.name: Armenian Bird Mosaic
guideSights.note: An impressive mosaic floor designed by Armenian Christian artists in about the 6th century. Call the Armenian Patriarchate of Jerusalem (+972 2 628 2331) to arrange a visit.

guideSights.name: Tombs of the Kings
guideSights.note: The burial site of Queen Helena of Adiabene, a 1st-century Jewish monarch. The site is owned by the State of France, and unfortunately cannot be visited except on rare occasions.

guideSights.name: Tomb of Simon the Just
guideSights.note: An ancient cave tomb, traditionally the burial site of Simeon the Just, a Jewish leader and high priest in the 3rd or 4th century BCE. If you cannot get to [[Upper Galilee#See

guideSights.name: Cave of the Minor Sanhedrin
guideSights.note: An ancient underground tomb with 23 niches, matching the 23 members of the "Minor Sanhedrin" (an ancient Jewish court).

guideSights.name: The Palestinian Heritage Museum
guideSights.note: Museum dedicated to Palestinian folkloric heritage.

guideSights.name: Ammunition Hill
guideSights.note: This was the main Jordanian fortification in East Jerusalem. Israel overran it in a bloody battle in 1967, leading to the capture of all of Jerusalem. Now the Israel Defense Force runs a museum here commemorating the battle.

guideSights.name: Hebrew University - Mount Scopus
guideSights.note: The humanities faculties of Hebrew University, Israel's top-ranked university, are located here. The campus is quiet and leafy, but confusing to navigate. There are impressive lookouts on the Old City to the south west and the Judaean Deser

guideSights.name: Tomb of Lazarus
guideSights.note: This Christian site is in Al Eizariya village, an eastern suburb of Jerusalem in the West Bank. Take bus 36, 63 or 263 from one of the Arab bus stations.

guideSights.name: Bethphage
guideSights.note: This is the place in which Jesus sent his disciples to find a donkey and a colt, upon which he would ride into Jerusalem. There is an annual Palm Sunday reenactment of Jesus' triumphal entry into Jerusalem which begins here.

guideSights.name: Tell el-Ful
guideSights.note: Archaeological digs have shown that this hill is the Biblical city of Gibeah, which was King Saul's capital before David came to the throne. The ancient ruins are not visible, but you can see a large ruined modern building. King Hussein of

guideSights.name: St. Elias Monastery
guideSights.note: An ancient Orthodox Christian monastery built over the ruins of a Byzantine church, surrounded by beautiful scenery.

guideSights.name: Mitzpeh Tel
guideSights.note: One of the nicest nature sites in Jerusalem, particularly in February-March when the blue lupines are blooming. It has a great view of the Old City and also (on clear days) all the way east to Jordan. A good site for a picnic.

guideSights.name: The Knesset
guideSights.note: The Israeli Parliament Building. The Knesset offers guided tours (in Hebrew, Arabic, English, French, Spanish, German, Russian, Amharic, Yiddish, and Finnish) for the public. Groups and individuals must call and arrange their guided tour in

guideSights.name: Supreme Court
guideSights.note: Located between the Knesset and the Central Bus Station, the Supreme Court building (opened 1992) is a mixture of traditional Jerusalem architecture and modern elements. Tours are available each weekday in Hebrew (11AM) and English (noon),

guideSights.name: Mount Herzl
guideSights.note: This is Israel's national cemetery and memorial. It contains the graves of Theodor Herzl and four prime ministers including Yitzhak Rabin. The Herzl Museum is in the entrance plaza. There are memorials for terror victims and MIA soldiers. N

guideSights.name: Yad Vashem
guideSights.note: Yad Vashem is Israel's Holocaust museum - documenting the Holocaust, preserving the stories of its six million victims, and teaching future generations through its archives, library, school, museums and recognition of the Righteous Among th

guideSights.name: HaPaamon military position
guideSights.note: A Jordanian military position from 1948-1967, on the flat land between Kibbutz Ramat Rachel and the Arab neighborhood Sur Baher. In 1967 it was conquered by Israeli forces who circumvented it and attacked it from behind. There is now a tall

guideSights.name: Israel Museum and the Shrine of the Book
guideSights.note: Israel's national museum sprawls over a compound near the Knesset and covers a broad body and extremely unique body of work in its five wings. The Judaica Wing contains an unequaled collection of Jewish ceremonial pieces, tools, and artwork

guideSights.name: Bible Lands Museum
guideSights.note: Laid out chronologically, the Bible Lands Museum provides a detailed look at the ancient societies of the Middle East. The museum's wide range of artifacts from around the region, including among others Egyptian, Minoan, and early Christian

guideSights.name: L.A. Mayer Memorial Museum of Islamic Art
guideSights.note: In the heart of Jewish West Jerusalem, this museum offers "one of the foremost collections of Islamic art" from across the Muslim world and the many centuries of Muslim artwork. It also contains an interesting collection of old watches and

guideSights.name: Wolfson Jewish Heritage Museum at Hechal Shlomo
guideSights.note: In the heart of downtown Jerusalem, this museum houses a unique collection of Jewish and Israeli art, with an interesting combination of old and new.

guideSights.name: Science Museum
guideSights.note: The museum features many "active exhibitions" which invite the visitor to touch and participate. A good choice for those travelling with kids.

guideSights.name: Museum on the Seam
guideSights.note: A museum which shows art with a socio-political emphasis. From 1948-1967 the only crossing between East and West Jerusalem was here.

guideSights.name: Begin Center
guideSights.note: A museum dedicated to the life and legacy of Menachem Begin, the first member of an opposition party to be elected as Israeli Prime Minister.

guideSights.name: Hebrew Music Museum
guideSights.note: A museum that describes the history of Jewish music across different time periods and cultures.

guideSights.name: Gush Katif Museum
guideSights.note: Gush Katif were the Jewish settlements in the Gaza Strip between 1967 and their evacuation in 2005. This small museum tells the history of Jewish settlement in the Gaza region from a right-wing perspective.

guideSights.name: Friends of Zion Museum
guideSights.note: This museum brings the stories of non-Jewish help and heroism to the world, who supported Zionism and stood bravely with the Jewish people. Visitors experience the unfolding story as though stepping back in time. Accompanied by a moving ori

guideSights.name: Levi Eshkol House
guideSights.note: Israel's Prime Ministers - Ben Gurion, Eshkol, and Golda Meir - lived here from 1950-1974. Now it is a museum about Israeli history and particularly Levi Eshkol's life. Reserve a visit before coming.

guideSights.name: Beit HaRav Kook
guideSights.note: The home of Rabbi Avraham Kook, chief rabbi of the Mandate of Palestine from 1921-1935, and the leading thinker of early religious Zionism. Visitors are given a pamphlet guiding them around the house, as well as a 20-minute movie in either

guideSights.name: Tax Museum
guideSights.note: Illustrates the history of taxation and its connection to society over thousands of years in Israel and other historic Jewish communities. Exhibits are labeled in Hebrew, but a guide can give a tour in English. Recommended to call ahead of

guideSights.name: Yemin Moshe
guideSights.note: The first neighborhood of Jerusalem to be built outside the Old City. The '''Mishkenot Sha'ananim''' housing project and the landmark '''windmill''' were finished in 1860; the rest of the neighborhood was built in the 1890s. Nowadays the ne

guideSights.name: Nachlaot
guideSights.note: A picturesque old neighborhood of narrow lanes and courtyards, built starting in 1875. Nowadays it has a distinctive character that is both religious and hipster. On evenings before the High Holidays, "selichot tours" here take you between

guideSights.name: German Colony
guideSights.note: A neighborhood southeast of the city center, founded in 1873 by German Protestants of the "Temple Society", who were expelled by the British during World War II. It's now an upscale residential neighborhood full of restored 19th century hom

guideSights.name: Baka
guideSights.note: Another neighborhood just south of the German Colony. This neighborhood has beautiful old Arab-style houses alongside new, modern buildings. There are many nice cafes on the main street of Derech Beit Lechem. This neighborhood too is home t

guideSights.name: Italian Synagogue
guideSights.note: The center of the Italian-origin Jewish community in Jerusalem. In addition to the synagogue, whose ancient wooden decorations were transferred from Italy and reassembled, there is a museum displaying beautiful art and Judaica. Shabbat pray

guideSights.name: Chagall Windows
guideSights.note: Famous stained glass windows by artist Marc Chagall in the synagogue of the Hadassah-Ein Kerem hospital.

guideSights.name: Ades Synagogue
guideSights.note: A beautifully painted synagogue built in 1901, the center of Israel's Syrian-Jewish community.

guideSights.name: Hesed VeRahamim Synagogue
guideSights.note: Built in 1925, this synagogue has a beautifully painted ceiling and interior. Even the outside doors have interesting metal carvings.

guideSights.name: Haas Promenade
guideSights.note: A park which has an incredible view of the Old City. It is common for tours to take people here blindfolded, and have them take off their blindfolds one by one to get their first view of the holy city.

guideSights.name: Gehinnom
guideSights.note: According to the Bible, this valley was once used for child sacrifice. Due to its association with evil, Gehinnom/Gehenna later became a name referring to Hell. Now, it is a pleasant though somewhat neglected park. If you come at night, you

guideSights.name: Farm in the Valley
guideSights.note: In the Gehinnom valley, a farm has been established with lots of animals that little kids will like to see, as well as activities for kids. A good family diversion.

guideSights.name: Ben Hinnom suspension bridge
guideSights.note: Israel's longest suspension bridge (200 meters) over the Gehinnom valley. Pedestrian only. Has nice views of the surroundings, and is only a little wobbly.

guideSights.name: Teddy Park
guideSights.note: Named after Teddy Kollek, Jerusalem mayor from 1965-1993, this park is located in the valley just below Jaffa Gate. The highlight is a fountain with 256 water spouts which performs a choreographed water show once every 2 hours (check the sc

guideSights.name: Independence Park
guideSights.note: The main park in Jerusalem's center city. A great place to relax or have a picnic.

guideSights.name: Gan HaPaamon
guideSights.note: The most visited park in Jerusalem, overlooking Mount Zion and the Old City. It features a replica of Philadelphia's Liberty Bell with the Biblical inscription - "Proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof".

guideSights.name: The Mifletzet
guideSights.note: This modern park is a landmark for Jerusalem kids. Its highlight is a giant monster with three tongues, each of which functions as a children's slide.

guideSights.name: Jerusalem Bird Observatory
guideSights.note: A small patch of wetlands, with a concealed location where you can watch birds without disturbing them. Interesting birds are probably most frequent during the spring and autumn migrations. You are encouraged to bring bird food (seeds and s

guideSights.name: Zion Square
guideSights.note: While small by international city square standards, this square is a common location for political rallies, concerts, street culture, and other events. The light rail runs through here without stopping; the Jaffa Center and City Hall statio

guideSights.name: Safra Square
guideSights.note: On Jaffa Street near the Old City. The square is surrounded by the municipality buildings (City Hall/"the ''Iriya''"). Concerts and events are sometimes held in the square.

guideSights.name: Chords Bridge
guideSights.note: Designed by starchitect Santiago Calatrava, this monumental bridge carries the light rail over a major intersection at the entrance to Jerusalem. The bridge covers a vast sweeping span supported only by metal chords stretched at oblique ang

guideSights.name: Jerusalem Biblical Zoo
guideSights.note: This zoo attracts more visitors than any other paid attraction in Israel. Decades ago, each animal was accompanied by descriptions of where it appeared in the Bible. However, nowadays there is not much Biblical about the zoo - it is simply

guideSights.name: Israel Aquarium
guideSights.note: Israel's only aquarium outside Eilat. Tickets must be purchased in advance for a specific entrance time. Entrance to the aquarium also lets you visit the butterfly/insect house which is next door (both aquarium and butterfly house are run b

guideSights.name: Sultan's Pool
guideSights.note: A large water reservoir just outside the Old City. It likely dates to the time of Herod, and has been remodeled since then. Now, it is empty of water, and used to hold concerts and other large events.

guideSights.name: Jerusalem YMCA
guideSights.note: A West Jerusalem landmark, built in 1933. There is a tower with views of the surroundings. The view is not bad, but less impressive than one might expect (you can see part of the Old City walls, and the top of Dome of the Rock, but little e

guideSights.name: Ramat Rachel
guideSights.note: A prominent hill guarding what used to be the southern approach to Jerusalem. In the First Temple period there was a royal palace here. Its remains, as well as some later archaeological findings, can be seen freely outside. In 1948, the hil

guideSights.name: Mamilla Cemetery
guideSights.note: Amid an old Muslim cemetery which contains graves of Muslim leaders, there is also a large ancient pool once used to hold water. The cemetery is now the center of some controversy, as the Center for Human Dignity (which will include the Mus

guideSights.name: Jason's Tomb
guideSights.note: A rock-cut tomb from the Maccabean period which belonged to someone named Jason, who once sailed to Egypt, according to an inscription. The tomb is freely accessible in a residential neighborhood, and well worth visiting if you are passing

guideSights.name: Chalcolithic village
guideSights.note: The remains of a 6000-year-old Chalcolithic village. Building ruins can be seen in a park just north of the Malcha shopping mall.

guideSights.name: Around the world in 92 days
guideSights.note: A multistory painting which depicts the world as seen from Jerusalem in "wide-eyed, childlike" form. Located on the wall of the Gerard Behar Center in Jerusalem. Cross to the north side of the street for a good view of the painting, with ex

guideSights.name: Hansen House
guideSights.note: This complex was established in 1887 as a walled-off hospital for patients with leprosy. Nowadays, the grounds form a park, while the building (which is quite beautiful, particularly its internal courtyard) hosts art exhibitions and cultura

guideSights.name: HaMiffal
guideSights.note: An art and cultural center, open to the public and featuring galleries, workshops, performances, and more.

guideSights.name: Mount Zion tunnel
guideSights.note: Between 1948 and 1967, West Jerusalem and Mount Zion were under Israeli control, but the only access between them was vulnerable to Jordanian sniper fire from the Old City walls. To avoid this fire, a secret tunnel was dug so that Mount Zio

guideSights.name: Motorcycle models
guideSights.note: In the heart of Jerusalem's most industrial district, one of the metalworkers has a hobby of making beautiful metal toy motorcycles which are displayed in his shop. Each model has a unique appearance and name, and if you speak Hebrew he'll

guideSights.name: Me'ah Shearim
guideSights.note: This neighborhood is perhaps the closest the 21st century can get to the shtetl Jewish communities of Eastern Europe. Minimally influenced by the modern world, the Hasidic residents of Me'ah Shearim continue to dress like their great-grandp

guideSights.name: Malchei Yisrael street
guideSights.note: A vibrant shopping street which forms the bouncing heart of Haredi Jerusalem. Especially on the evenings preceding the Sabbath and major holidays, and on summer nights, it is one of the busiest areas of the city. The street, with its narrow

guideSights.name: Tombs of the Sanhedrin
guideSights.note: A freely accessible park with impressive rock-carved tombs from the 1st century. The most impressive tombs are deeper (further north) in the park.

guideSights.name: Lifta

guideSights.note: Blocks of residential buildings which are built from prefabricated dodecahedral units, resembling a beehive.

guideSights.name: 9/11 Living Memorial Plaza
guideSights.note: A memorial to the victims of the 9/11 attacks in the US. On a rural forested hill within Jerusalem city limits.

guideSights.note: Franciscan church and monastery

guideSights.name: Gorny Convent
guideSights.note: A Russian Orthodox convent dating to the 19th century

guideSights.name: Me'ah Shearim

guideSights.name: Malchei Yisrael street

guideSights.name: The Knesset
guideSights.note: The Israeli Parliament Building. The Knesset offers guided tours (in Hebrew, Arabic, English, French, Spanish, German, Russian, Amharic, Yiddish, and Finnish) for the public. Groups and individuals must call and arrange their guided tour in

guideSights.name: Supreme Court
guideSights.note: Located between the Knesset and the Central Bus Station, the Supreme Court building (opened 1992) is a mixture of traditional Jerusalem architecture and modern elements. Tours are available each weekday in Hebrew (11AM) and English (noon),

guideSights.name: Mount Herzl
guideSights.note: This is Israel's national cemetery and memorial. It contains the graves of Theodor Herzl and four prime ministers including Yitzhak Rabin. The Herzl Museum is in the entrance plaza. There are memorials for terror victims and MIA soldiers. N

guideSights.name: Yad Vashem
guideSights.note: Yad Vashem is Israel's Holocaust museum - documenting the Holocaust, preserving the stories of its six million victims, and teaching future generations through its archives, library, school, museums and recognition of the Righteous Among th

guideSights.name: HaPaamon military position
guideSights.note: A Jordanian military position from 1948-1967, on the flat land between Kibbutz Ramat Rachel and the Arab neighborhood Sur Baher. In 1967 it was conquered by Israeli forces who circumvented it and attacked it from behind. There is now a tall

guideSights.name: Israel Museum and the Shrine of the Book
guideSights.note: Israel's national museum sprawls over a compound near the Knesset and covers a broad body and extremely unique body of work in its five wings. The Judaica Wing contains an unequaled collection of Jewish ceremonial pieces, tools, and artwork

guideSights.name: Bible Lands Museum
guideSights.note: Laid out chronologically, the Bible Lands Museum provides a detailed look at the ancient societies of the Middle East. The museum's wide range of artifacts from around the region, including among others Egyptian, Minoan, and early Christian

guideSights.name: L.A. Mayer Memorial Museum of Islamic Art
guideSights.note: In the heart of Jewish West Jerusalem, this museum offers "one of the foremost collections of Islamic art" from across the Muslim world and the many centuries of Muslim artwork. It also contains an interesting collection of old watches and

guideSights.name: Wolfson Jewish Heritage Museum at Hechal Shlomo
guideSights.note: In the heart of downtown Jerusalem, this museum houses a unique collection of Jewish and Israeli art, with an interesting combination of old and new.

guideSights.name: Science Museum
guideSights.note: The museum features many "active exhibitions" which invite the visitor to touch and participate. A good choice for those travelling with kids.

guideSights.name: Museum on the Seam
guideSights.note: A museum which shows art with a socio-political emphasis. From 1948-1967 the only crossing between East and West Jerusalem was here.

guideSights.name: Begin Center
guideSights.note: A museum dedicated to the life and legacy of Menachem Begin, the first member of an opposition party to be elected as Israeli Prime Minister.

guideSights.name: Hebrew Music Museum
guideSights.note: A museum that describes the history of Jewish music across different time periods and cultures.

guideSights.name: Gush Katif Museum
guideSights.note: Gush Katif were the Jewish settlements in the Gaza Strip between 1967 and their evacuation in 2005. This small museum tells the history of Jewish settlement in the Gaza region from a right-wing perspective.

guideSights.name: Friends of Zion Museum
guideSights.note: This museum brings the stories of non-Jewish help and heroism to the world, who supported Zionism and stood bravely with the Jewish people. Visitors experience the unfolding story as though stepping back in time. Accompanied by a moving ori

guideSights.name: Levi Eshkol House
guideSights.note: Israel's Prime Ministers - Ben Gurion, Eshkol, and Golda Meir - lived here from 1950-1974. Now it is a museum about Israeli history and particularly Levi Eshkol's life. Reserve a visit before coming.

guideSights.name: Beit HaRav Kook
guideSights.note: The home of Rabbi Avraham Kook, chief rabbi of the Mandate of Palestine from 1921-1935, and the leading thinker of early religious Zionism. Visitors are given a pamphlet guiding them around the house, as well as a 20-minute movie in either

guideSights.name: Tax Museum
guideSights.note: Illustrates the history of taxation and its connection to society over thousands of years in Israel and other historic Jewish communities. Exhibits are labeled in Hebrew, but a guide can give a tour in English. Recommended to call ahead of

guideSights.name: Yemin Moshe
guideSights.note: The first neighborhood of Jerusalem to be built outside the Old City. The '''Mishkenot Sha'ananim''' housing project and the landmark '''windmill''' were finished in 1860; the rest of the neighborhood was built in the 1890s. Nowadays the ne

guideSights.name: Nachlaot
guideSights.note: A picturesque old neighborhood of narrow lanes and courtyards, built starting in 1875. Nowadays it has a distinctive character that is both religious and hipster. On evenings before the High Holidays, "selichot tours" here take you between

guideSights.name: German Colony
guideSights.note: A neighborhood southeast of the city center, founded in 1873 by German Protestants of the "Temple Society", who were expelled by the British during World War II. It's now an upscale residential neighborhood full of restored 19th century hom

guideSights.name: Baka
guideSights.note: Another neighborhood just south of the German Colony. This neighborhood has beautiful old Arab-style houses alongside new, modern buildings. There are many nice cafes on the main street of Derech Beit Lechem. This neighborhood too is home t

guideSights.name: Italian Synagogue
guideSights.note: The center of the Italian-origin Jewish community in Jerusalem. In addition to the synagogue, whose ancient wooden decorations were transferred from Italy and reassembled, there is a museum displaying beautiful art and Judaica. Shabbat pray

guideSights.name: Chagall Windows
guideSights.note: Famous stained glass windows by artist Marc Chagall in the synagogue of the Hadassah-Ein Kerem hospital.

guideSights.name: Ades Synagogue
guideSights.note: A beautifully painted synagogue built in 1901, the center of Israel's Syrian-Jewish community.

guideSights.name: Hesed VeRahamim Synagogue
guideSights.note: Built in 1925, this synagogue has a beautifully painted ceiling and interior. Even the outside doors have interesting metal carvings.

guideSights.name: Haas Promenade
guideSights.note: A park which has an incredible view of the Old City. It is common for tours to take people here blindfolded, and have them take off their blindfolds one by one to get their first view of the holy city.

guideSights.name: Gehinnom
guideSights.note: According to the Bible, this valley was once used for child sacrifice. Due to its association with evil, Gehinnom/Gehenna later became a name referring to Hell. Now, it is a pleasant though somewhat neglected park. If you come at night, you

guideSights.name: Farm in the Valley
guideSights.note: In the Gehinnom valley, a farm has been established with lots of animals that little kids will like to see, as well as activities for kids. A good family diversion.

guideSights.name: Ben Hinnom suspension bridge
guideSights.note: Israel's longest suspension bridge (200 meters) over the Gehinnom valley. Pedestrian only. Has nice views of the surroundings, and is only a little wobbly.

guideSights.name: Teddy Park
guideSights.note: Named after Teddy Kollek, Jerusalem mayor from 1965-1993, this park is located in the valley just below Jaffa Gate. The highlight is a fountain with 256 water spouts which performs a choreographed water show once every 2 hours (check the sc

guideSights.name: Independence Park
guideSights.note: The main park in Jerusalem's center city. A great place to relax or have a picnic.

guideSights.name: Gan HaPaamon
guideSights.note: The most visited park in Jerusalem, overlooking Mount Zion and the Old City. It features a replica of Philadelphia's Liberty Bell with the Biblical inscription - "Proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof".

guideSights.name: The Mifletzet
guideSights.note: This modern park is a landmark for Jerusalem kids. Its highlight is a giant monster with three tongues, each of which functions as a children's slide.

guideSights.name: Jerusalem Bird Observatory
guideSights.note: A small patch of wetlands, with a concealed location where you can watch birds without disturbing them. Interesting birds are probably most frequent during the spring and autumn migrations. You are encouraged to bring bird food (seeds and s

guideSights.name: Zion Square
guideSights.note: While small by international city square standards, this square is a common location for political rallies, concerts, street culture, and other events. The light rail runs through here without stopping; the Jaffa Center and City Hall statio

guideSights.name: Safra Square
guideSights.note: On Jaffa Street near the Old City. The square is surrounded by the municipality buildings (City Hall/"the ''Iriya''"). Concerts and events are sometimes held in the square.

guideSights.name: Chords Bridge

guideSights.name: Jerusalem Biblical Zoo
guideSights.note: This zoo attracts more visitors than any other paid attraction in Israel. Decades ago, each animal was accompanied by descriptions of where it appeared in the Bible. However, nowadays there is not much Biblical about the zoo - it is simply

guideSights.name: Israel Aquarium
guideSights.note: Israel's only aquarium outside Eilat. Tickets must be purchased in advance for a specific entrance time. Entrance to the aquarium also lets you visit the butterfly/insect house which is next door (both aquarium and butterfly house are run b

guideSights.name: Sultan's Pool
guideSights.note: A large water reservoir just outside the Old City. It likely dates to the time of Herod, and has been remodeled since then. Now, it is empty of water, and used to hold concerts and other large events.

guideSights.name: Jerusalem YMCA
guideSights.note: A West Jerusalem landmark, built in 1933. There is a tower with views of the surroundings. The view is not bad, but less impressive than one might expect (you can see part of the Old City walls, and the top of Dome of the Rock, but little e

guideSights.name: Ramat Rachel
guideSights.note: A prominent hill guarding what used to be the southern approach to Jerusalem. In the First Temple period there was a royal palace here. Its remains, as well as some later archaeological findings, can be seen freely outside. In 1948, the hil

guideSights.name: Mamilla Cemetery
guideSights.note: Amid an old Muslim cemetery which contains graves of Muslim leaders, there is also a large ancient pool once used to hold water. The cemetery is now the center of some controversy, as the Center for Human Dignity (which will include the Mus

guideSights.name: Jason's Tomb
guideSights.note: A rock-cut tomb from the Maccabean period which belonged to someone named Jason, who once sailed to Egypt, according to an inscription. The tomb is freely accessible in a residential neighborhood, and well worth visiting if you are passing

guideSights.name: Chalcolithic village
guideSights.note: The remains of a 6000-year-old Chalcolithic village. Building ruins can be seen in a park just north of the Malcha shopping mall.

guideSights.name: Around the world in 92 days
guideSights.note: A multistory painting which depicts the world as seen from Jerusalem in "wide-eyed, childlike" form. Located on the wall of the Gerard Behar Center in Jerusalem. Cross to the north side of the street for a good view of the painting, with ex

guideSights.name: Hansen House
guideSights.note: This complex was established in 1887 as a walled-off hospital for patients with leprosy. Nowadays, the grounds form a park, while the building (which is quite beautiful, particularly its internal courtyard) hosts art exhibitions and cultura

guideSights.name: HaMiffal
guideSights.note: An art and cultural center, open to the public and featuring galleries, workshops, performances, and more.

guideSights.name: Mount Zion tunnel

guideSights.name: Motorcycle models
